extracted.intended_audience: readers and contributors to Popular Science Monthly (scientists, naturalists, archaeologists, engineers, and the educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: A miscellany/notes section of a 19th-century popular-science magazine containing short reviews, technical guidance (e.g., lightning-rod construction), reports of scientific observations, and solicitations for contributions to an institutional archaeological volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lightning-rod: minimum copper stem diameter
rubrics_metrics.description: The main stem of a copper lightning-conductor should never be less than -fa of an inch diameter; this dimension is not sufficient for a building more than eighty feet high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification sets a lower bound on conductor thickness and notes height-related adequacy (i.e., same minimum may be insufficient for taller buildings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lightning-rod: use and sizing of galvanized iron vs. copper
rubrics_metrics.description: Galvanized iron may be used instead of copper, but then the diameter must be greater in the ratio of 6.7 to 2.5, the conducting capacity of iron being to that of copper as 14 to 77.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If substituting galvanized iron for copper, increase cross-section according to the stated ratio to compensate for lower conductivity; account for conducting-capacity differences in material choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lightning-rod: galvanized iron rope and strip minimum dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: A galvanized iron-rope conductor should never be less than j% of an inch diameter; a galvanized iron strip should be 4 inches wide and \ of an inch thick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using galvanized-iron rope or strip, adhere to the specified minimum diameter/width/thickness dimensions to ensure adequate conducting capacity (original text contains typographic numerals; follow printed spec).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lightning-rod: continuity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A lightning-rod must be continuous and unbroken from end to end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conductor path must be electrically continuous without breaks to provide an effective path to ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lightning-rod: attachment method to buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: A rod need not be attached to a building by insulated fastenings; metal clamps may be safely employed, provided the rod be of good conducting capacity and otherwise efficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insulated fastenings are unnecessary if clamps and the conductor maintain good conducting capacity and the overall installation is otherwise sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lightning-rod: termination points
rubrics_metrics.description: Above, the rod must terminate in metal points, well projected into the air; these points should be multiple and perfectly sharp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminate conductors with multiple, sharply pointed metal tips projecting into free air to improve performance (multiple points preferred).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lightning-rod: grounding / earth contact
rubrics_metrics.description: The bottom of the conductor must be carried down into the earth and be connected with it by a surface-contact of large extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a broad-area connection to earth (large surface contact) rather than a minimal point contact to dissipate charge effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lightning-rod: metallic connection of large metal masses (with exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: All large masses of metal in a building should be metallically connected with the lightning-rod, except when they are liable to be occupied by people during a thunder-storm — an iron balcony, for instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bond large metallic masses to the conductor to avoid alternative arcing paths, but avoid bonding items (e.g., balconies) that people might occupy during storms to reduce risk of creating a dangerous current path through occupants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smithsonian solicitation: subjects sought for North American archaeology
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors of the Smithsonian Institution invite cooperation and information concerning American archaeology and enumerate the ancient monuments and subjects to be described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Institution specifically requests information/descriptions about: mounds and earthworks; shell-heaps; cave and cliff dwellings; masonry; sculptured slabs or carved images; inscriptions; rock-paintings; graves and cemeteries; aboriginal quarries; salt-works; caches or deposits of objects in large quantities; workshops or places of ancient aboriginal industry; ancient roads or trails; reservoirs and aqueducts. Contributors should provide original records, descriptions, and relevant observations for these subject types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smithsonian solicitation: documentary and collection materials requested
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to original records and descriptions, the Smithsonian desires copies of all books, memoirs, pamphlets, extracts from periodicals, and newspaper clippings related to American archaeology, and information on all collections of American antiquities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit copies of published/unpublished literature and descriptive inventories of any private or public collections (however small); applicants may request the Institution's 'Circular in Reference to American Archaeology' for detailed instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for a useful practical manual (Mineralogy example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good practical manual is remarkable for the profuseness and neatness of its crystallographic illustrations and is designed for practical working miners, quarrymen, field-geologists, and students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuals intended for practitioners should prioritize clear, abundant, and neat illustrations and be targeted to the needs of working professionals and students (audience-appropriate scope and presentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agricultural primer vs. comprehensive treatment (First Principles of Agriculture example)
rubrics_metrics.description: An introductory primer that summarizes elementary scientific facts and principles is serviceable to those seeking an introduction, but scientific agriculture requires study with thoroughness and mastery before practical and safe application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and evaluators should recognize the limits of abridged primers and expect more comprehensive works for practitioners; practical application of agricultural science demands deeper study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for reporting a new microscopic organism (Dallinger example)
rubrics_metrics.description: An account of a newly observed microscopic organism should detail its life-history, morphology (shape, flagella placement), modes of locomotion and attachment, observed division/self-division processes, transformations (e.g., flagellate to amoeboid), and tolerances (e.g., temperature survivability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical descriptions should include careful continuous observation of behavior and reproduction, quantitative size estimates, morphological details, life-cycle stages, and experimental notes (e.g., temperature effects), so readers can evaluate and reproduce findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of high-quality illustrations in paleontological memoirs
rubrics_metrics.description: The intrinsic value of a paleontological memoir is enhanced by truly admirable lithographic plates by which the text is illustrated and adorned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality lithographic or equivalent plates are important for paleontological descriptions and increase the utility and authority of the work; include clear, accurate plates when describing fossils.
